claim: At postsynaptic sites of neurons, a prominent clathrin-coated structure, the endocytic zone (EZ), controls the trafficking of glutamate receptors.
source: At postsynaptic sites of neurons, a prominent clathrin-coated structure, the endocytic zone (EZ), controls the trafficking of glutamate receptors and is essential for synaptic plasticity.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a foundational claim about the EZ function, supported by the broader literature context.

claim: The endocytic zone is essential for synaptic plasticity.
source: At postsynaptic sites of neurons, a prominent clathrin-coated structure, the endocytic zone (EZ), controls the trafficking of glutamate receptors and is essential for synaptic plasticity.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by citations in the introduction.

claim: A subset of endocytic proteins only transiently appeared at postsynaptic sites.
source: We found that a subset of endocytic proteins only transiently appeared at postsynaptic sites.
evidence: This is supported by live-cell imaging data showing differential dynamics of endocytic proteins (Figure 5).

claim: Other proteins were persistently enriched and partitioned at the edge of the EZ.
source: In contrast, other proteins were persistently enriched and partitioned at the edge of the EZ.
evidence: This is supported by super-resolution microscopy data showing spatial organization of endocytic proteins (Figure 6).

claim: Uncoupling the EZ from the synapse led to the loss of most of these components.
source: We found that uncoupling the EZ from the synapse led to the loss of most of these components, while disrupting interactions with the actin cytoskeleton or membrane did not alter EZ positioning.
evidence: This is supported by Shank knockdown experiments (Figure 7).

claim: Disrupting interactions with the actin cytoskeleton or membrane did not alter EZ positioning.
source: We found that uncoupling the EZ from the synapse led to the loss of most of these components, while disrupting interactions with the actin cytoskeleton or membrane did not alter EZ positioning.
evidence: This is supported by pharmacological and genetic manipulation experiments (Figure 7).

claim: Plasticity-inducing stimuli promoted the reorganization of the EZ.
source: Finally, we found that plasticity-inducing stimuli promoted the reorganization of the EZ.
evidence: This is supported by cLTP and cLTD experiments (Figure 8).

claim: The EZ is a stable, highly organized molecular platform where components are differentially recruited and positioned to orchestrate the endocytosis of synaptic receptors.
source: We conclude that the EZ is a stable, highly organized molecular platform where components are differentially recruited and positioned to orchestrate the endocytosis of synaptic receptors.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from multiple lines of experimental evidence presented in the manuscript.

claim: Clathrin-mediated endocytosis is the principal mechanism for the internalization of membrane components in mammalian cells.
source: Clathrin-mediated endocytosis is the principal mechanism for the internalization of membrane components, and is essential for cellular homeostasis, intercellular signaling, and nutrient uptake in mammalian cells (Kaksonen and Roux, 2018; McMahon and Boucrot, 2011; Mettlen et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: Clathrin-mediated endocytosis is essential for cellular homeostasis, intercellular signaling, and nutrient uptake in mammalian cells.
source: Clathrin-mediated endocytosis is the principal mechanism for the internalization of membrane components, and is essential for cellular homeostasis, intercellular signaling, and nutrient uptake in mammalian cells (Kaksonen and Roux, 2018; McMahon and Boucrot, 2011; Mettlen et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: Clathrin-mediated endocytosis involves the tightly controlled initiation and maturation of clathrin-coated pits mediated by the sequential recruitment of clathrin, cargo, and endocytic adaptor proteins.
source: This process involves the tightly controlled initiation and maturation of clathrin-coated pits that is mediated by the sequential recruitment of clathrin, cargo, and endocytic adaptor proteins (Cocucci et al., 2012; Taylor et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: Well-characterized clathrin coats are small (~100 nm) and short-lived (<120 sec).
source: Apart from these well-characterized, small (~100 nm) and short-lived ( < 120 sec) clathrin coats, numerous electron and (live-cell) light microscopy studies have revealed that clathrin can assemble into a remarkably large variety of membrane-attached structures (Grove et al., 2014; Heuser, 1980; Leyton-Puig et al., 2017; Saffarian et al., 2009; Sanan and Anderson, 1991).
evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: Clathrin can assemble into a remarkably large variety of membrane-attached structures.
source: Apart from these well-characterized, small (~100 nm) and short-lived ( < 120 sec) clathrin coats, numerous electron and (live-cell) light microscopy studies have revealed that clathrin can assemble into a remarkably large variety of membrane-attached structures (Grove et al., 2014; Heuser, 1980; Leyton-Puig et al., 2017; Saffarian et al., 2009; Sanan and Anderson, 1991).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple microscopy studies.

claim: Clathrin structures vary from 100 nm up to 1 µm with lifetimes ranging from seconds to tens of minutes.
source: Clathrin structures varying from 100 nm up to 1 µm with lifetimes ranging from seconds to tens of minutes have been reported.
evidence: This is stated as a summary of reported observations from the literature.

claim: The EZ is stably associated with the postsynaptic density (PSD).
source: At postsynaptic sites, a clathrin-coated structure (CCS) referred to as the endocytic zone (EZ) is stably associated with the postsynaptic density (PSD) (Blanpied et al., 2002; Lu et al., 2007), via a Shank-Homer1c-Dynamin3 interaction (Lu et al., 2007; Rosendale et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The EZ is associated with the PSD via a Shank-Homer1c-Dynamin3 interaction.
source: At postsynaptic sites, a clathrin-coated structure (CCS) referred to as the endocytic zone (EZ) is stably associated with the postsynaptic density (PSD) (Blanpied et al., 2002; Lu et al., 2007), via a Shank-Homer1c-Dynamin3 interaction (Lu et al., 2007; Rosendale et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Disrupting the PSD-EZ interaction severely affects glutamate receptor levels at synapses.
source: Disrupting the PSD-EZ interaction severely affects glutamate receptor levels at synapses.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: AMPA-type glutamate receptors undergo trafficking mediated by the EZ.
source: Particularly, the ionotropic AMPA-type glutamate receptors (Petrini et al., 2009; Rosendale et al., 2017) and metabotropic glutamate receptors (Scheefhals et al., 2019) have been found to undergo trafficking mediated by the EZ, while transferrin receptors are not preferentially internalized near the synapse (Rosendale et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Metabotropic glutamate receptors undergo trafficking mediated by the EZ.
source: Particularly, the ionotropic AMPA-type glutamate receptors (Petrini et al., 2009; Rosendale et al., 2017) and metabotropic glutamate receptors (Scheefhals et al., 2019) have been found to undergo trafficking mediated by the EZ, while transferrin receptors are not preferentially internalized near the synapse (Rosendale et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Transferrin receptors are not preferentially internalized near the synapse.
source: Particularly, the ionotropic AMPA-type glutamate receptors (Petrini et al., 2009; Rosendale et al., 2017) and metabotropic glutamate receptors (Scheefhals et al., 2019) have been found to undergo trafficking mediated by the EZ, while transferrin receptors are not preferentially internalized near the synapse (Rosendale et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Once internalized at the EZ, glutamate receptors enter the local recycling mechanism that retains receptors in intracellular pools that can recycle back to the synaptic membrane in an activity-dependent manner.
source: It has been proposed that once internalized at the EZ, glutamate receptors enter the local recycling mechanism, that retains receptors in intracellular pools that can recycle back to the synaptic membrane in an activity-dependent manner (Park et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study and is presented as a proposed mechanism.

claim: The local recycling of receptors via the EZ is essential for synaptic plasticity.
source: Indeed, the local recycling of receptors via the EZ is essential for synaptic plasticity as uncoupling the EZ from the PSD depletes synaptic AMPA receptors and aborts activity-induced trafficking of receptors to the synaptic membrane during long-term potentiation (Lu et al., 2007; Petrini et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Uncoupling the EZ from the PSD depletes synaptic AMPA receptors and aborts activity-induced trafficking of receptors to the synaptic membrane during long-term potentiation.
source: Indeed, the local recycling of receptors via the EZ is essential for synaptic plasticity as uncoupling the EZ from the PSD depletes synaptic AMPA receptors and aborts activity-induced trafficking of receptors to the synaptic membrane during long-term potentiation (Lu et al., 2007; Petrini et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Disruptions in EZ structure and function have been associated with the development of neuronal disorders such as autism spectrum disorder and Parkinson's disease.
source: Importantly, disruptions in EZ structure and function have been associated with the development of neuronal disorders such as autism spectrum disorder and Parkinson's disease (Cortese et al., 2016; Scheefhals et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: 75% ± 5% of dendritic spines contained a distinct EZ.
source: In dendrites, a high density of clathrin structures was found in the shaft and the majority of dendritic spines contained a distinct EZ, defined as a clathrin puncta closely associated with the PSD (75% ± 5%), consistent with previous observations (Blanpied et al., 2002; Lu et al., 2007; Scheefhals et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from the experimental data.

claim: Labeling endogenous CLCa using a CRISPR/Cas9-based approach resulted in comparable distribution of clathrin structures.
source: Importantly, labeling endogenous CLCa using a CRISPR/Cas9-based approach (Willems et al., 2020) resulted in comparable distribution of clathrin structures (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: STED resolved individual structures at much higher resolution than confocal, often resolving distinct substructures within clathrin patches that appeared homogenous in confocal microscopy.
source: Notably, STED resolved individual structures at much higher resolution than confocal, often resolving distinct substructures within clathrin patches that appeared homogenous in confocal microscopy (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by comparison of confocal and STED images in Figure 1.

claim: 59% ± 5% of the PSDs were associated with one clathrin structure.
source: We found that 59% ± 5% of the PSDs were associated with one clathrin structure, while 14% ± 2% and 5.4% ± 0.8% were associated with two or three clathrin structures, respectively (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from the experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: 14% ± 2% of PSDs were associated with two clathrin structures.
source: We found that 59% ± 5% of the PSDs were associated with one clathrin structure, while 14% ± 2% and 5.4% ± 0.8% were associated with two or three clathrin structures, respectively (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from the experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: 5.4% ± 0.8% of PSDs were associated with three clathrin structures.
source: We found that 59% ± 5% of the PSDs were associated with one clathrin structure, while 14% ± 2% and 5.4% ± 0.8% were associated with two or three clathrin structures, respectively (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from the experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Dendritic clathrin structures range in size from as small as 0.01 µm2 up to 0.43 µm2.
source: Next, we analyzed the morphology of dendritic clathrin structures and found a large range of sizes from as small as 0.01 µm2 up to 0.43 µm2 (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from the experimental data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: The average area of PSD-associated clathrin structures was lower, albeit not statistically different from the average area of clathrin structures found in the shaft.
source: On average, the area of PSD-associated clathrin structures was lower, albeit not statistically different from the average area of clathrin structures found in the shaft (area clathrin structures in shaft: 0.045 ± 0.003 µm2, spine: 0.038 µm2 ± 0.002, p > 0.1).
evidence: This is a quantitative comparison from the experimental data.

claim: The variability in sizes of clathrin structures in the shaft was much larger than in spines.
source: However, the variability in sizes of clathrin structures in the shaft, was much larger than in spines (CV shaft: 1.3; spines: 0.84), with larger structures exclusively found in the shaft and not in spines (Figure 1D and E; range in width/length shaft: 0.15 µm to 1.7 µm, spine: 0.084 µm to 0.78 µm).
evidence: This is a quantitative comparison from the experimental data shown in Figure 1D and E.

claim: Large clathrin structures were regularly observed in the shaft, approximately ~3 per 20 µm of dendrite.
source: Indeed, large clathrin structures were regularly observed in the shaft, approximately ~3 per 20 µm of dendrite (data not shown).
evidence: This is a quantitative observation from the experimental data.

claim: There was no correlation between size and circularity in dendritic clathrin structures (R2 = 0.006).
source: However, there was no correlation between size and circularity in dendritic clathrin structures (R2 = 0.006).
evidence: This is a quantitative analysis from the experimental data.

claim: The dendritic shaft predominantly contained stationary CCSs.
source: The dendritic shaft predominantly contained stationary CCSs, however smaller anterograde and retrograde moving puncta were also observed (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by live-cell imaging data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Fast-moving particles in the dendritic shaft were small (IQR: 0.013–0.065 µm2) most likely reflecting intracellular vesicle transport.
source: Interestingly, these fast-moving particles were small (IQR: 0.013–0.065 µm2) most likely reflecting intracellular vesicle transport.
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement with an interpretation based on size.

claim: The EZ appeared much more stable than dendritic clathrin structures, with little fluctuations in GFP-CLCa intensity (CV: 0.02).
source: In spines, the EZ appeared much more stable than dendritic clathrin structures, with little fluctuations in GFP-CLCa intensity (CV: 0.02, Figure 2C: upper panel).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from live-cell imaging data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The fluctuations in intensity of clathrin structures in shaft and spines were significantly different, with much lower fluctuations found in spines (shaft CV: 0.06 ± 0.004, spine CV: 0.02 ± 0.001, p < 0.001).
source: On average, the fluctuations in intensity of clathrin structures in shaft and spines were significantly different, with much lower fluctuations found in spines (shaft CV: 0.06 ± 0.004, spine CV: 0.02 ± 0.001, p < 0.001) (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is a quantitative comparison with statistical significance from the experimental data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: CCSs in spines had a considerably higher average lifetime compared to CCSs in the shaft (average lifetime spines: 10 ± 0.7 min, shaft: 6.0 ± 0.3 minutes, p < 0.001).
source: Longer acquisitions of 20 min at 30-s intervals showed that the CCSs in spines had a considerably higher average lifetime compared to CCSs in the shaft (average lifetime spines: 10 ± 0.7 min, shaft: 6.0 ± 0.3 minutes, p < 0.001) (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is a quantitative comparison with statistical significance from the experimental data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: 68.1% ± 6.0% of PSDs remained associated with at least one clathrin structure that was present for the entire 20 min.
source: Indeed, 68.1% ± 6.0% of PSDs remained associated with at least one clathrin structure that was present for the entire 20 min, confirming that the EZ is stably coupled to the PSD (Blanpied et al., 2002; Lu et al., 2007; Scheefhals et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from the experimental data.

claim: In the dendritic shaft, only a small fraction (~15%) of CCSs was long-lived (>17.5 min).
source: In contrast, in the dendritic shaft, only a small fraction (~15%) of CCSs was long-lived ( > 17.5 min) and the median lifetime of all events was ~2.5 min, indicating that the majority of CCSs in the dendritic shaft are transient structures (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from the experimental data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: The median lifetime of all CCS events in the dendritic shaft was ~2.5 min.
source: In contrast, in the dendritic shaft, only a small fraction (~15%) of CCSs was long-lived ( > 17.5 min) and the median lifetime of all events was ~2.5 min, indicating that the majority of CCSs in the dendritic shaft are transient structures (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from the experimental data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: In stable shaft structures GFP-CLCa recovered relatively fast (tau: 13.0 min) to 75.8% ± 10% in 20 min.
source: We determined that in stable shaft structures GFP-CLCa recovered relatively fast (tau: 13.0 min) to 75.8% ± 10% in 20 min (Figure 2G and H), indicating a high level of clathrin exchange at these structures.
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from FRAP experiments shown in Figure 2G and H.

claim: The EZ showed relatively low levels of turnover (tau: 36.2 min) and total recovery (38.2% ± 5.2% after 20 min).
source: In contrast to the high turnover of stationary structures in the shaft, the EZ showed relatively low levels of turnover (tau: 36.2 min) and total recovery (38.2% ± 5.2% after 20 min) (Figure 2G and H), suggesting little exchange of clathrin at the EZ.
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from FRAP experiments shown in Figure 2G and H.

claim: The centroid of the EZ was generally located within 100 nm from the border of the PSD.
source: We found that the centroid of the EZ was generally located within 100 nm from the border of the PSD (Figure 3C) with an average border-to-centroid distance from PSD to EZ of 10.6 ± 7.8 nm, confirming that the EZ is closely linked to the PSD and well within a distance that can be linked by scaffold proteins (Lu et al., 2007).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from SMLM data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The average border-to-centroid distance from PSD to EZ was 10.6 ± 7.8 nm.
source: We found that the centroid of the EZ was generally located within 100 nm from the border of the PSD (Figure 3C) with an average border-to-centroid distance from PSD to EZ of 10.6 ± 7.8 nm, confirming that the EZ is closely linked to the PSD and well within a distance that can be linked by scaffold proteins (Lu et al., 2007).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from SMLM data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The average area of the EZ was 35.0 ± 2.0 × 10³ nm².
source: On average the area of the EZ was 35.0 ± 2.0 × 103 nm2 (Figure 3E), and 224.6 ± 10.4 nm in length and 146.5 ± 5.2 nm in width (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from SMLM data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: The EZ was 224.6 ± 10.4 nm in length and 146.5 ± 5.2 nm in width.
source: On average the area of the EZ was 35.0 ± 2.0 × 103 nm2 (Figure 3E), and 224.6 ± 10.4 nm in length and 146.5 ± 5.2 nm in width (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from SMLM data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The dimensions (length and width) of individual EZ structures were positively correlated (R² = 0.58).
source: Moreover, the dimensions (length and width) of individual structures were positively correlated (R2 = 0.58).
evidence: This is a quantitative analysis from SMLM data.

claim: Secondary, smaller clathrin structures were between 50 and 100 nm in diameter.
source: The secondary, smaller structures were between 50 and 100 nm in diameter (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C), similar to the reported size of endocytic vesicles (Kirchhausen and Harrison, 1981; Pearse and Crowther, 1987).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from SMLM data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The size of secondary clathrin structures is similar to the reported size of endocytic vesicles.
source: The secondary, smaller structures were between 50 and 100 nm in diameter (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C), similar to the reported size of endocytic vesicles (Kirchhausen and Harrison, 1981; Pearse and Crowther, 1987).
evidence: This is a comparison to literature values supported by citations.

claim: 66.8% ± 6.9% of PSDs was associated with GFP-CLCa.
source: In this experiment, we found that 66.8% ± 6.9% of PSDs was associated with GFP-CLCa (Figure 4A and C).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from the experimental data shown in Figure 4A and C.

claim: The fraction of PSDs associated with HIP1R, β2-adaptin, Dyn2, CPG2, Eps15, and Itsn1L was similar to the percentage of clathrin-associated PSDs.
source: We found that the fraction of PSDs associated with HIP1R, β2-adaptin, Dyn2, CPG2, Eps15, and Itsn1L was similar to the percentage of clathrin-associated PSDs.
evidence: This is a comparison of quantitative measurements from the experimental data.

claim: PICALM, Epsn2, Amph, and FCHO1 were less frequently found in association with the PSD.
source: In contrast, PICALM, Epsn2, Amph, and FCHO1 were less frequently found in association with the PSD (Figure 4B and C).
evidence: This is a comparison of quantitative measurements from the experimental data shown in Figure 4B and C.

claim: Endogenously tagged Eps15, Itsn1 and Dyn2 showed a similar distribution and perisynaptic localization as found in the exogenous expression experiments.
source: Importantly, for endogenously tagged Eps15, Itns1 and Dyn2 we found a similar distribution and perisynaptic localization as we found in the exogenous expression experiments (Figure 4D, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by comparison of knockin and overexpression data shown in Figure 4D and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Endogenous labeling using antibodies for Eps15, Itsn1, and Dyn2 confirmed that these proteins are located at perisynaptic sites.
source: Similarly, endogenous labeling using antibodies for Eps15, Itsn1, and Dyn2 confirmed that these proteins are located at perisynaptic sites (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by immunocytochemistry data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Endocytic proteins accumulated either briefly (<3 min) or appeared persistent (>9 min) at perisynaptic sites.
source: Endocytic proteins accumulated either briefly ( < 3 min) or appeared persistent ( > 9 min) at perisynaptic sites (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is a quantitative observation from live-cell imaging data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: HIP1R, β2-adaptin, Dyn2, CPG2, Eps15, and Itsn1L are stable components that are generally long-lived.
source: These data also indicated that HIP1R, β2-adaptin, Dyn2, CPG2, Eps15, and Itsn1L are stable components that are generally long-lived (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the lifetime distribution data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: The average lifetime of FCHO1 at perisynaptic sites was 2.74 ± 1.7 min.
source: In contrast, the average lifetimes of FCHO1 (2.74 ± 1.7 min), PICALM (1.73 ± 0.20 min), Epsn2 (3.00 ± 0.20 min), and Amph (2.73 ± 1.7 min) at perisynaptic sites were significantly lower compared to the average lifetime of CLCa.
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from live-cell imaging data.

claim: The average lifetime of PICALM at perisynaptic sites was 1.73 ± 0.20 min.
source: In contrast, the average lifetimes of FCHO1 (2.74 ± 1.7 min), PICALM (1.73 ± 0.20 min), Epsn2 (3.00 ± 0.20 min), and Amph (2.73 ± 1.7 min) at perisynaptic sites were significantly lower compared to the average lifetime of CLCa.
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from live-cell imaging data.

claim: The average lifetime of Epsn2 at perisynaptic sites was 3.00 ± 0.20 min.
source: In contrast, the average lifetimes of FCHO1 (2.74 ± 1.7 min), PICALM (1.73 ± 0.20 min), Epsn2 (3.00 ± 0.20 min), and Amph (2.73 ± 1.7 min) at perisynaptic sites were significantly lower compared to the average lifetime of CLCa.
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from live-cell imaging data.

claim: The average lifetime of Amph at perisynaptic sites was 2.73 ± 1.7 min.
source: In contrast, the average lifetimes of FCHO1 (2.74 ± 1.7 min), PICALM (1.73 ± 0.20 min), Epsn2 (3.00 ± 0.20 min), and Amph (2.73 ± 1.7 min) at perisynaptic sites were significantly lower compared to the average lifetime of CLCa.
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from live-cell imaging data.

claim: The lifetime of short-lived endocytic protein events is comparable to the duration of endocytic events (~2 min).
source: Notably, the lifetime of these short-lived events is comparable to the duration of endocytic events (~2 min), suggesting that these proteins are transiently recruited upon the induction of endocytosis.
evidence: This is a comparison with an interpretation based on the data.

claim: All endocytic proteins except CPG2 showed considerably higher turnover than clathrin.
source: Except for CPG2, all endocytic proteins showed considerably higher turnover than clathrin (percentage of recovery after 10 min CPG2: 29.4% ± 3.7%, HIP1R: 59.2% ± 5.2%, β2-adaptin: 56.7% ± 3.8%, Eps15: 88.1 ± 3.8, Itsn1L: 93.9 ± 8.7) (Figure 5E, Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a quantitative comparison from FRAP experiments shown in Figure 5E and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Eps15, β2-adaptin, and Itsn1L were often distributed in smaller patches around and sometimes within the EZ marked by CLCa.
source: Strikingly, we found that β2-adaptin, Eps15, and Itsn1L were often distributed in smaller patches around and sometimes within the EZ marked by CLCa (Figure 6A–C).
evidence: This is supported by SMLM data shown in Figure 6A–C.

claim: HIP1R showed a more homogenous distribution and often colocalized with the EZ entirely and even surrounding the EZ.
source: HIP1R showed a more homogenous distribution and often colocalized with the EZ entirely and even surrounding the EZ (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is supported by SMLM data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: All the endocytic proteins analyzed peaked within 25 nm from the edge of the clathrin structure.
source: We first mapped the absolute distance of localizations to the border of the EZ averaged over a population of EZs and found that all the endocytic proteins analyzed here peaked within 25 nm from the edge of the clathrin structure (Figure 6F).
evidence: This is a quantitative analysis from SMLM data shown in Figure 6F.

claim: The relative density of Eps15, β2-adaptin, and Itsn1L peaked within the EZ, but close to the edge of the EZ.
source: When analyzing the endocytic adaptor proteins relative to the EZ, we again found that the relative density of Eps15, β2-adaptin, and Itsn1L peaked within the EZ, but close to the edge of the EZ (Figure 6I).
evidence: This is a quantitative analysis from SMLM data shown in Figure 6I.

claim: The profiles of HIP1R and Dyn2 localizations showed less clear peaks, indicating a more homogenous distribution of these proteins within the EZ.
source: The profiles of HIP1R and Dyn2 localizations (Figure 6G) showed less clear peaks, indicating a more homogenous distribution of these proteins within the EZ.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the localization profile data shown in Figure 6G.

claim: Shank knockdown reduced the number of clathrin-positive PSDs (0.5 ± 0.1 relative to control).
source: Indeed, we found that Shank-KD did not only reduce the number of clathrin-positive PSDs as found before (0.5 ± 0.1 relative to control), but also reduced the association of the PSD with other endocytic proteins (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from Shank knockdown experiments shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Shank-KD significantly reduced Homer1c-Eps15 (0.63 ± 0.1), Homer1c-Itsn1L (0.6 ± 0.1) and Homer1c-β2-adaptin (0.55 ± 0.1) coupling compared to control.
source: We found that Shank-KD significantly reduced Homer1c-Eps15 (0.63 ± 0.1), Homer1c-Itsn1L (0.6 ± 0.1) and Homer1c-β2-adaptin (0.55 ± 0.1) coupling compared to control (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from Shank knockdown experiments shown in Figure 7B.

claim: HIP1R (0.89 ± 0.04), Dyn2 (0.91 ± 0.1), and CPG2 (0.86 ± 0.1) were not uncoupled from the PSD after Shank-KD.
source: Interestingly, HIP1R (0.89 ± 0.04), Dyn2 (0.91 ± 0.1), and CPG2 (0.86 ± 0.1) were not uncoupled from the PSD (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from Shank knockdown experiments shown in Figure 7B.

claim: PSD-EZ coupling via Shank proteins is necessary for the integrity of the EZ.
source: Together, these findings show that PSD-EZ coupling via Shank proteins is necessary for the integrity of the EZ.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the Shank knockdown experiments.

claim: Latrunculin B slightly decreased the PSD-EZ association (0.81 ± 0.1), but this was not statistically significant.
source: The actin depolymerization drug Latrunculin B slightly decreased the PSD-EZ association (0.81 ± 0.1), but this was not statistically significant.
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from pharmacological experiments.

claim: The Arp2/3 inhibitor CK-666 (0.98 ± 0.1) did not significantly alter PSD-EZ association.
source: The Arp2/3 inhibitor CK-666 (0.98 ± 0.1) also did not significantly alter PSD-EZ association (Figure 7D and F), suggesting that disrupting actin dynamics does not disrupt positioning of the EZ.
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from pharmacological experiments shown in Figure 7D and F.

claim: Jasplakinolide resulted in significantly more PSD-EZ association compared to control (1.27 ± 0.04, p < 0.05).
source: Jasplakinolide, an F-actin stabilizing drug, resulted in significantly more PSD-EZ association compared to control (1.27 ± 0.04, p < 0.05).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement with statistical significance from pharmacological experiments.

claim: Overexpression of a clathrin-light chain mutant that is unable to bind HIP1R (GFP-CLCb-EED/QQN) did not affect the localization of the EZ.
source: Overexpression of a clathrin-light chain mutant that is unable to bind HIP1R (GFP-CLCb-EED/QQN) (Chen and Brodsky, 2005; Poupon et al., 2008), did not affect the localization of the EZ (Figure 7E and F), further indicating that coupling to the actin cytoskeleton is not a primary mechanism for maintaining the EZ.
evidence: This is supported by overexpression experiments shown in Figure 7E and F.

claim: Knockdown of endogenous CPG2 did not affect PSD-EZ coupling.
source: However, knockdown of endogenous CPG2 using established shRNAs (Cottrell et al., 2004) did not affect PSD-EZ coupling (Figure 7E).
evidence: This is supported by knockdown experiments shown in Figure 7E.

claim: Overexpression of a mutant form of the AP2 mu2 subunit that is unable to interact with PIP2 (AP2m2-P1) did not change the fraction of EZ-positive PSDs (1.1 ± 0.1).
source: To address this, we overexpressed a mutant form of the AP2 mu2 subunit that is unable to interact with PIP2 (AP2m2-P1) and was shown to hamper receptor internalization (Raman et al., 2014), but we found no change in the fraction of EZ-positive PSDs (1.1 ± 0.1), suggesting that coupling to the membrane via AP2-PIP2 interactions does not affect EZ maintenance (Figure 7E and F).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from overexpression experiments shown in Figure 7E and F.

claim: Itsn1L knockdown did not alter the fraction of EZ-positive PSDs.
source: However, Itsn1L knockdown did not alter the fraction of EZ-positive PSDs (Figure 7E and F).
evidence: This is supported by knockdown experiments shown in Figure 7E and F.

claim: The EZ is assembled from a distinct set of endocytic proteins and is maintained and positioned primarily by interactions with the PSD.
source: Altogether, based on these mechanistic experiments, we conclude that the EZ is assembled from a distinct set of endocytic proteins and is maintained and positioned primarily by interactions with the PSD.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from multiple mechanistic experiments.

claim: Induction of mGluR-LTD by a 5 minute-application of DHPG significantly increased the number of PSDs associated with multiple CCSs (control: 0.95 ± 0.1, 5' DHPG: 2.1 ± 0.4).
source: We found that induction of mGluR-LTD by a 5 minute-application of DHPG, significantly increased the number of PSDs associated with multiple CCSs (control: 0.95 ± 0.1, 5' DHPG: 2.1 ± 0.4).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from plasticity experiments.

claim: The effect of DHPG on PSDs associated with multiple CCSs was transient and returned to control levels after 10 min.
source: Strikingly, the effect of DHPG was transient and the number of PSDs associated with multiple CCSs returned to control levels after 10 min (Figure 8A and B).
evidence: This is a quantitative observation from plasticity experiments shown in Figure 8A and B.

claim: The effect of DHPG was blocked by the selective mGluR5 antagonist MPEP.
source: This effect was blocked by the selective mGluR5 antagonist MPEP, indicating that this effect was mediated by mGluR5 activation.
evidence: This is supported by pharmacological experiments.

claim: Application of NMDA had only a small, non-significant effect (control: 1.03 ± 0.08, 5' NMDA: 1.47 ± 0.19).
source: Intriguingly, application of NMDA had only a small, non-significant effect (control: 1.03 ± 0.08, 5' NMDA: 1.47 ± 0.19), indicating that these protocols differentially affect the perisynaptic CCSs.
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from plasticity experiments.

claim: cLTP resulted in an increase in the number of PSDs containing multiple CCSs 30 min after induction (control: 17.6% ± 2.8%, 30' cLTP: 29.1% ± 2.7%, p < 0.01).
source: We found that cLTP resulted in an increase in the number of PSDs containing multiple CCSs 30 min after induction (control: 17.6% ± 2.8%, 30' cLTP: 29.1% ± 2.7%, p < 0.01).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement with statistical significance from plasticity experiments.

claim: The effect of cLTP on PSDs containing multiple CCSs was long-lasting, up to 2 hr after cLTP induction.
source: Remarkably, in contrast to cLTD this effect was long-lasting, up to 2 hr after cLTP induction (Figure 8E).
evidence: This is a quantitative observation from plasticity experiments shown in Figure 8E.

claim: The effect of cLTP was blocked in the presence of AP5, an NMDAR antagonist.
source: The effect was blocked in the presence of AP5, an NMDAR antagonist, indicating that the observed effect is NMDAR-mediated (Figure 8F).
evidence: This is supported by pharmacological experiments shown in Figure 8F.

claim: The appearance of new CCSs was preferentially observed at PSDs that increased in size in response to the cLTP protocol.
source: Interestingly, we noted that the appearance of new CCSs was preferentially observed at PSDs that increased in size in response to the cLTP protocol, while PSDs that were not associated with multiple CCS after 30 min remained the same size (Figure 8H).
evidence: This is a quantitative observation from live-cell imaging experiments shown in Figure 8H.

claim: CLCa area was not different between control and cLTP (control: 0.06 ± 0.007, cLTP: 0.05 ± 0.009).
source: We found that CLCa area was not different between control and cLTP (control: 0.06 ± 0.007, cLTP: 0.05 ± 0.009) (Figure 8I).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from plasticity experiments shown in Figure 8I.

claim: Live-cell confocal imaging showed that CLCa intensity was not affected after cLTP.
source: Similarly, live-cell confocal imaging showed that CLCa intensity was not affected after cLTP (Figure 8J), indicating that there is no recruitment of clathrin to spines, but suggests that the EZ undergoes remodeling, or perhaps splits in response to synaptic activity.
evidence: This is a quantitative observation from live-cell imaging experiments shown in Figure 8J.

claim: Synaptic activity patterns that induce long-term alterations in synaptic strength are accompanied by structural reorganization of the perisynaptic endocytic machinery at excitatory synapses.
source: These data show that synaptic activity patterns that induce long-term alterations in synaptic strength are accompanied by structural reorganization of the perisynaptic endocytic machinery at excitatory synapses.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the plasticity experiments.

claim: The EZ is a highly unique clathrin structure that contains a defined arsenal of endocytic proteins.
source: Here, we present evidence that the EZ is a highly unique clathrin structure that contains a defined arsenal of endocytic proteins, is differentially retained at the EZ and highly organized at the nanoscale level with respect to the clathrin assembly.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion drawn from multiple lines of experimental evidence.

claim: The EZ is reorganized in response to synaptic activity.
source: Moreover, we show that the EZ is reorganized in response to synaptic activity.
evidence: This is supported by plasticity experiments.

claim: CCSs in the dendritic shaft form a highly heterogenous population.
source: While CCSs in the dendritic shaft form a highly heterogenous population, including small, fast-moving particles, as well as larger stationary structures, the EZ is remarkably stable with little variation from spine to spine.
evidence: This is a summary of observations from live-cell imaging and morphological analysis.

claim: The EZ is remarkably stable with little variation from spine to spine.
source: While CCSs in the dendritic shaft form a highly heterogenous population, including small, fast-moving particles, as well as larger stationary structures, the EZ is remarkably stable with little variation from spine to spine.
evidence: This is a summary of observations from live-cell imaging and morphological analysis.

claim: The heterogeneity in the dendritic shaft likely resembles CCSs found in other cell types.
source: This heterogeneity in the dendritic shaft likely resembles CCSs found in other cell types, where small clathrin structures represent transient endocytic pits or intracellular vesicles while the large patches are stable, membrane-attached structures (Grove et al., 2014; Leyton-Puig et al., 2017; Saffarian et al., 2009).
evidence: This is an interpretation based on comparison to literature.

claim: Based on the morphological and dynamic behavior of clathrin, the EZ can be distinguished from other clathrin assemblies found in the dendritic shaft.
source: Together, these results indicate that based on the morphological and dynamic behavior of clathrin, the EZ can be distinguished from other clathrin assemblies found in the dendritic shaft.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from morphological and dynamic analysis.

claim: The early-phase endocytic proteins β2-adaptin, Eps15, and Itsn1L are stable EZ residents that localize preferentially at the edge of the EZ.
source: Based on our live-cell imaging, quantitative super-resolution imaging and mechanistic studies, we conclude that the early-phase endocytic proteins β2-adaptin, Eps15, and Itsn1L are stable EZ residents that localize preferentially at the edge of the EZ, which is surprisingly similar to findings on flat clathrin lattices in non-neuronal cells (Sochacki et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from multiple experimental approaches.

claim: The localization of β2-adaptin, Eps15, and Itsn1L at the edge of the EZ is surprisingly similar to findings on flat clathrin lattices in non-neuronal cells.
source: Based on our live-cell imaging, quantitative super-resolution imaging and mechanistic studies, we conclude that the early-phase endocytic proteins β2-adaptin, Eps15, and Itsn1L are stable EZ residents that localize preferentially at the edge of the EZ, which is surprisingly similar to findings on flat clathrin lattices in non-neuronal cells (Sochacki et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a comparison to literature findings supported by a citation.

claim: The accumulation of the AP-2 complex and its binding partner Eps15 at the periphery of the EZ likely contributes to the efficient capture of cargoes and their local uptake via endocytosis.
source: The accumulation of the AP-2 complex and its binding partner Eps15 at the periphery of the EZ, likely contributes to the efficient capture of cargoes, that is synaptic membrane proteins, and their local uptake via endocytosis.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the functional significance of the spatial organization.

claim: Itsn1 facilitates mGluR-mediated AMPAR trafficking.
source: In addition, we recently reported that Itsn1, a multi-domain scaffold protein that coordinates different aspects of endocytosis (Pechstein et al., 2010; Evergren et al., 2007; Hussain et al., 2001), also facilitates mGluR-mediated AMPAR trafficking (van Gelder et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a recent study.

claim: Removing Shank proteins specifically uncoupled the early-phase proteins.
source: Furthermore, removing Shank proteins, which was previously shown to uncouple the EZ from the PSD (Lu et al., 2007; Scheefhals et al., 2019), specifically uncoupled the early-phase proteins, indicating that these proteins are indeed stable residents and coupled to the EZ.
evidence: This is supported by Shank knockdown experiments.

claim: The later-phase proteins HIP1R, Dyn2, and CPG2 were stably associated with the EZ, but this association seemed independent of PSD-EZ coupling via Shank.
source: The later-phase proteins HIP1R, Dyn2, and CPG2 were also stably associated with the EZ, but this association seemed independent of PSD-EZ coupling via Shank.
evidence: This is supported by Shank knockdown experiments showing these proteins were not uncoupled.

claim: The clear differential localization patterns of Dyn2 between different EZs may indicate that Dyn2 relocates to the EZ upon endocytosis.
source: For Dyn2 we found that in most cases, the distribution of Dyn2 at the EZ was diffuse, but the clear differential localization patterns between different EZs may indicate that Dyn2 relocates to the EZ upon endocytosis as has been suggested before (Rosendale et al., 2017).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the SMLM data with support from a citation.

claim: The later-phase proteins are not directly coupled to the EZ under basal conditions but rather preferentially reside in close proximity via other interactions.
source: Taken together, it is likely that the later-phase proteins are not directly coupled to the EZ under basal conditions but rather preferentially reside in close proximity via other interactions.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the Shank knockdown and localization data.

claim: PICALM, FCHO1, Epsn2, and Amph are only transiently recruited to the EZ upon induction of endocytosis.
source: Finally, we found that PICALM, FCHO1, Epsn2, and Amph were associated with the EZ to a much lesser extent and appeared only transiently at perisynaptic sites. Interestingly, Amph, Epsn2, and FCHO1 are BAR proteins, and preferentially bind curved membranes. Thus, perhaps these proteins are only transiently recruited to the EZ upon induction of endocytosis and the associated increase in membrane curvature.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the dynamics and properties of these proteins.

claim: AP2 is not involved in EZ coupling to the membrane or membrane anchoring is not a prerequisite for EZ positioning.
source: We found that expression of a dominant-negative form of AP2-mu2 that interferes with the clathrin-PIP2 binding did not abrogate EZ positioning, suggesting that AP2 is not involved in EZ coupling to the membrane or membrane anchoring is not a prerequisite for EZ positioning.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the AP2m2-P1 overexpression experiments.

claim: Abrogating EZ-actin cytoskeletal interactions did not disrupt the localization of the EZ at perisynaptic sites.
source: Similarly, we found that abrogating EZ-actin cytoskeletal interactions, did not disrupt the localization of the EZ at perisynaptic sites.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from multiple experiments targeting actin interactions.

claim: Although CPG2 and HIP1R are stable EZ residents they are not involved in maintaining the EZ.
source: However, removing CPG2 or interfering with the HIP1R-Clathrin interaction did not disrupt the localization of the EZ, suggesting that although CPG2 and HIP1R are stable EZ residents they are not involved in maintaining the EZ.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from CPG2 knockdown and CLCb-EED/QQN overexpression experiments.

claim: The actin cytoskeleton does not seem to have a prime structural role in maintaining or positioning the EZ.
source: Thus, the actin cytoskeleton does not seem to have a prime structural role in maintaining or positioning the EZ.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from multiple experiments targeting actin interactions.

claim: NMDAR-LTD and mGluR-LTD trigger different signaling pathways and internalize distinct pools of AMPARs.
source: Interestingly, while both NMDAR-LTD and mGluR-LTD lead to a reduction of surface AMPARs, activation of NMDARs and mGluRs trigger different signaling pathways and internalize distinct pools of AMPARs (Casimiro et al., 2011; Oliet et al., 1997; Waung et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: LTP is associated with increased endocytic flux.
source: Nevertheless, a recent computational study suggested that also LTP is associated with increased endocytic flux (Sumi and Harada, 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a computational study.

claim: cLTP was associated with the appearance of multiple clathrin-coated pits per PSD.
source: Similarly, an EM study showed that cLTP was associated with the appearance of multiple clathrin-coated pits per PSD (Puchkov et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to an EM study.

claim: LTP-induced internalization of SK channels contributes to synaptic potentiation.
source: Moreover, it has been shown that LTP-induced internalization of SK channels contributes to synaptic potentiation (Lin et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: The reorganization of perisynaptic CCSs might facilitate changes in endocytic rate and modulate LTP induction and maintenance.
source: Thus, perhaps the reorganization of perisynaptic CCSs facilitates changes in endocytic rate and modulates LTP induction and maintenance.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the functional significance of EZ reorganization.

claim: On longer time scales, the reorganization of spine CCSs might endow potentiated spines with the ability to more readily recycle synaptic receptors.
source: On longer time scales, the reorganization of spine CCSs might endow potentiated spines with the ability to more readily recycle synaptic receptors and thus respond more efficiently to changes in synaptic activity.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the functional significance of EZ reorganization.

claim: The EZ is a highly organized clathrin structure where endocytic proteins are differentially retained and stabilized.
source: Taken all together, we found that the EZ is a highly organized clathrin structure where endocytic proteins are differentially retained and stabilized.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion drawn from multiple lines of experimental evidence.

claim: The distinct organization of the EZ likely facilitates the efficient capture and endocytosis of synaptic membrane proteins close to the PSD.
source: This distinct organization likely facilitates the efficient capture and endocytosis of synaptic membrane proteins close to the PSD.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the functional significance of the EZ organization.

claim: The EZ is reorganized in response to synaptic activity for the first time.
source: Moreover, for the first time, we show that the EZ is reorganized in response to synaptic activity.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the finding supported by experimental data.

claim: Hippocampal cultures were prepared from brain of embryonic day 18 (E18) Wistar rats.
source: Hippocampal cultures were prepared from brain of embryonic day 18 (E18) Wistar rats (both genders) as described before (Scheefhals et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a methodological detail supported by a citation.

claim: Neurons were transfected at DIV11-16 using Lipofectamine 2000.
source: At DIV11-16 neurons were transfected with indicated constructs using Lipofectamine 2000 (Invitrogen).
evidence: This is a methodological detail.

claim: For the knock-ins transfection was performed at DIV3.
source: For the knock-ins transfection was performed at DIV3.
evidence: This is a methodological detail.
